analysis.one_liner: Requires the largest banks to phase out all financing of fossil fuel projects by 2030.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a vote in either chamber; it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require banks with $50 billion or more in assets to submit plans to the Federal Reserve to cut the greenhouse gas emissions tied to their lending and investing in half by 2030 and to zero by 2050. It would ban them from financing new or expanded fossil fuel projects within 60 days of passage, thermal coal by 2025, and all fossil fuel financing by 2030. Banks that failed to comply could face fines, forced divestment, or loss of deposit insurance for their bank subsidiaries. It also directs regulators to study how the transition affects workers and communities.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the bill would cut the flow of bank money into new oil, gas, and coal projects, reducing the emissions that drive climate change — a benefit spread broadly across the public, and especially to low-income and minority communities the bill says suffer disproportionate harm from financed pollution. It would also push banks to prioritize severance and retraining lending for fossil fuel workers whose jobs the transition would eliminate.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities exposed to climate and pollution harms

how_it_helps.text: Covered banks must submit Federal Reserve-approved plans to reach zero financed emissions by 2050 and cut financed emissions 50% by 2030, with plans that cannot rely on carbon offsets. [S2] [S3]
Financing of new or expanded fossil fuel projects would be prohibited 60 days after enactment, thermal coal financing by 2025, and all fossil fuel financing by 2030. [S2] [S3]

Plans must prioritize withdrawing funding from companies with disproportionate impacts on low-income and minority communities, and lending for severance, retraining, and other benefits for workers displaced by the transition. [S3]
Noncompliant banks face penalties, mandatory divestiture, and possible loss of federal deposit insurance, giving the requirements real teeth. [S2] [S3]
The Federal Reserve must report on financed emissions systemwide and on the needs of workers and communities affected by the transition, including options such as a public investment bank. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Large bank holding companies ($50 billion and up) would lose a major line of business — lending to and underwriting for oil, gas, and coal companies and projects — and would bear the cost of restructuring their portfolios. Energy companies would face a shrinking pool of bank financing, which could raise their cost of capital and, in some cases, the prices of the energy they produce. Supporters argue these costs are far smaller than the damages from climate change itself.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large banks and fossil fuel companies

drawbacks.text: Banning all fossil fuel financing by 2030 — including infrastructure like pipelines and refineries — could constrain energy supply and raise financing costs, and energy costs fall hardest on lower-income households. An honest supporter would acknowledge this transition-cost risk. [S3]

The mandate reaches any bank holding company over $50 billion in assets and any company deriving 15% of revenue from fossil fuels, a broad net that critics argue reaches well beyond the biggest climate offenders. [S3]

Compliance depends heavily on Federal Reserve discretion: the Fed writes the regulations, accepts or rejects each plan, and sets penalties, so the strength of the law would hinge on how future Fed boards interpret it. [S3]
The bill's deepest cuts are timed after key dates (2030 and 2050), meaning most of the burden falls on future Congresses and future regulators to sustain enforcement. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a hard phaseout of fossil fuel finance with real enforcement (divestiture orders, deposit-insurance leverage) and explicit protections for displaced workers, which addresses the fairest objection — that energy workers and energy prices would bear the transition's costs. But the all-source fossil fuel ban by 2030 is aggressive, would concentrate costs on banks and energy producers, and could raise some consumer energy prices in the short run. The benefit is a large reduction in the banking system's role in funding projects that drive climate change; the costs are real but narrower and borne mostly by the industries being restricted.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Markey introduced the Fossil Free Finance Act on March 30, 2023, with Sens. Merkley and Sanders. [S3]
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee on the day of introduction. [S1] [S5]
The bill never received any further action — no committee markup, no floor vote — and died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025. [S1] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large banks and fossil fuel companies are better off: the financing restrictions never took effect, so the status quo of bank lending to fossil fuel projects continued. Communities exposed to climate and pollution harms gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large banks and fossil fuel producers

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Banking Committee.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Joined Markey in introducing the bill at introduction.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Joined Markey in introducing the bill at introduction.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Large banks and the fossil fuel industry
against.what_they_did: Had strong financial stakes in blocking the bill; the bill attracted no Republican support and never advanced past referral.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. All five cosponsors were Democrats or the independent Sen. Sanders, with no Republican support, so the bill's coalition was entirely progressive, but no formal partisan opposition was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Large bank holding companies ($50B+ in assets)
industries.note: The bill would prohibit them from financing new fossil fuel projects almost immediately and all fossil fuel financing by 2030, eliminating a profitable line of lending and underwriting. Their interest in the bill's defeat ran against the public benefit of cutting financed emissions.

The bill would cut off bank financing for new or expanded projects — wells, pipelines, terminals, refineries — and thermal coal by 2025, raising their cost of capital. Because their revenue depends on continued fossil fuel expansion, their interest was opposed to the bill's climate aims.

industries.industry: Coalition-driven bank fossil fuel lending (underwriting and syndication)
industries.note: The bill's definition of financed emissions reaches underwriting, securitization, derivatives, and market making, so it would restructure how capital markets finance energy projects, not just bank loans.
